facts.claim: Microplastics were found in the blood of humans, with 88% being fragments and 79% being white/clear.
facts.quote: The MPs were predominantly categorised as fragments (88 %) and were white/clear (79 %).

facts.claim: Microplastic pollution in the placenta is linked to a 5.06 increased risk of intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR).
facts.quote: Microplastic pollution in the placenta significantly increases the risk of intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) (95 % CI: 2. 07-8. 06; OR: 5. 06).

facts.claim: Microplastics were detected in human placenta and fetal meconium, with sizes ranging from 2.1 to 100 micrometers.
facts.quote: The results of the included studies confirmed the existence of microplastics with varying sizes (2. 1 to 100 micrometers) in the placenta and the fetal body.

facts.claim: Placental microplastic levels are linked to reduced birthweights and 1-minute Apgar scores.
facts.quote: One reported placental microplastic levels correlated with reduced birthweights and 1-minute Apgar scores.

facts.claim: Microplastics were found in 4 out of 6 human placentas, with 5 in the fetal side, 4 in the maternal side and 3 in the chorioamniotic membranes.
facts.quote: In total, 12 microplastic fragments (ranging from 5 to 10 μm in size), with spheric or irregular shape were found in 4 placentas (5 in the fetal side, 4 in the maternal side and 3 in the chorioamniotic membranes)

facts.claim: Consuming food in plastic containers is linked to a 5.39 increased chance of microplastic contamination in pregnant women.
facts.quote: the results showed that consuming food in plastic containers increased the chance of contamination with microplastics in pregnant women (95 % CI: 1. 32-21. 9; OR: 5. 39).

research.angle: Microplastics are present in human blood and placenta, and while their presence is linked to reduced birthweights and intrauterine growth restriction, the full scope of health effects remains under investigation.
research.verdict: The evidence confirms that microplastics are present in human blood and reproductive tissues, with some correlations to adverse pregnancy outcomes.
research.caveat: Many studies are small-scale or observational, and more large-scale investigations are needed to confirm the specific hazards and health impacts.
